questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A freehold estate in real property is characterized by:

answers.text: a fixed rental period with no ownership rights
the right to use the property only for a specific government-approved purpose
an ownership interest of indefinite or potentially perpetual duration
temporary possession that terminates automatically at the holder's death

explanations.a: A fixed rental period describes a leasehold estate, not a freehold.
explanations.b: Government-use approval is a zoning concept, not a characteristic of freehold ownership.
explanations.c: A freehold estate is an ownership interest whose duration is either perpetual (fee simple) or measured by a life, both of which are indefinite as opposed to a fixed term.
explanations.d: Termination at death describes a life estate, which is just one form of freehold; freehold generally means duration is not fixed in advance by agreement.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: An owner holds title to a parcel 'so long as it is used as a school.' If the property is ever used for another purpose, title automatically reverts to the grantor. This type of estate is BEST described as:

answers.text: a fee simple absolute
a fee simple defeasible
a life estate measured by the grantee's life
an estate for years

explanations.a: Fee simple absolute has no conditions attached; the ownership is complete and unconditional.
explanations.b: A fee simple defeasible (or fee simple determinable) is a freehold ownership subject to a condition whose violation causes the estate to end and revert to the grantor.
explanations.c: A life estate ends at the measuring life's death, not upon violation of a use condition.
explanations.d: An estate for years is a leasehold with a fixed term, not a conditional freehold.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: To create a valid joint tenancy with the right of survivorship, all four unities must be present simultaneously. Which of the following correctly lists all four unities?

answers.text: time, title, interest, and possession
possession, use, income, and management control
value, duration, alienability, and purpose
title, occupancy, equity interest, and transferability

explanations.a: The four unities of joint tenancy are time (acquired simultaneously), title (same instrument), interest (equal shares), and possession (right to possess the whole).
explanations.b: Use, income, and management control are ownership rights but are not the recognized four unities of joint tenancy.
explanations.c: Value, duration, alienability, and purpose are not the four unities of joint tenancy.
explanations.d: Occupancy, equity interest, and transferability are not the correct terms for the four unities.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: Unlike joint tenants, tenants in common have the right to:

answers.text: automatically inherit the deceased co-owner's share by right of survivorship
exclude other co-owners from using any portion of the common property
collect a disproportionately larger share of rental income than their ownership percentage
convey their individual ownership share to a third party without the other co-owners' consent

explanations.a: Right of survivorship belongs to joint tenants, not tenants in common; a tenant-in-common's share passes through the estate.
explanations.b: Each co-owner in a tenancy in common has the right to possess the entire property; no co-owner can lawfully exclude the others.
explanations.c: Each tenant in common is entitled to income proportional to their ownership share, not a larger amount.
explanations.d: A tenant in common may freely sell, mortgage, or devise their undivided share without the other co-owners' approval.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: In a standard condominium arrangement, the unit owner typically holds:

answers.text: title to the land beneath the entire building structure
ownership of the entire building in which the unit is located
fee simple title to the unit's interior airspace and an undivided interest in common elements
a proprietary lease rather than any form of fee simple ownership

explanations.a: The land and structural elements are common elements owned by all unit owners together, not solely by any single owner.
explanations.b: No single unit owner holds title to the entire building.
explanations.c: A condominium owner has fee simple title to the interior airspace of the unit and a proportional undivided interest in common areas such as hallways, grounds, and roof.
explanations.d: A proprietary lease describes cooperative housing (co-ops), not condominiums; condos provide fee ownership.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A leasehold estate grants the tenant:

answers.text: permanent ownership of the real property
the right to possess and use the property for a defined period
an equity interest that grows as rent is paid over time
the ability to encumber the property with a mortgage lien

explanations.a: Permanent ownership describes a freehold estate, not a leasehold.
explanations.b: A leasehold gives the tenant the right of possession and use for a period set by the lease, without conveying ownership.
explanations.c: Paying rent does not create equity ownership; equity is built through ownership, not tenancy.
explanations.d: Only the fee owner may mortgage the property; a tenant cannot encumber title through a mortgage.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: Under a gross lease, the tenant pays a fixed periodic rent, and the landlord is responsible for:

answers.text: paying most or all of the operating expenses of the property
sharing net income from the property with the tenant each month
reimbursing the tenant for all utility costs at year-end
contributing to a shared reserve account for tenant improvements

explanations.a: In a gross lease, the landlord bears most operating expenses — taxes, insurance, maintenance — out of the fixed rent received.
explanations.b: Sharing net income with the tenant is a feature of a percentage lease, not a gross lease.
explanations.c: Utility reimbursement at year-end is not a characteristic of a gross lease; the landlord simply pays expenses.
explanations.d: A tenant-improvement reserve is a lease negotiation item; it does not define a gross lease.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: For a lease to be valid and enforceable, it generally must contain all of the following EXCEPT:

answers.text: an adequate description of the leased premises
the duration of the tenancy
the rental amount agreed upon by the parties
a clause specifying the tenant's business or professional occupation

explanations.a: The premises must be identified so both parties know what is being leased.
explanations.b: Without a duration, the tenancy would be indefinite and the nature of the leasehold unclear.
explanations.c: Rent is the consideration that supports the lease; without it, the agreement may lack mutuality.
explanations.d: A tenant's occupation or profession is not an essential element of lease validity; leases are generally enforceable without it.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: Under the implied warranty of habitability in a residential lease, a landlord is generally required to:

answers.text: fully renovate the unit's interior between each tenancy
maintain the premises in a safe and livable condition throughout the lease term
guarantee the tenant's personal safety from all criminal acts on the premises
replace all appliances and fixtures whenever newer models become commercially available

explanations.a: A full renovation between tenancies is not required; the landlord must maintain the existing condition as habitable.
explanations.b: The implied warranty of habitability requires the landlord to keep the residential unit in a condition fit for human habitation — including adequate heat, water, and structural soundness.
explanations.c: While landlords may have a duty of reasonable care, guaranteeing protection from all criminal acts is beyond the scope of the implied warranty of habitability.
explanations.d: No law requires appliance upgrades to latest models as a condition of habitability.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A landlord's persistent failure to repair the heating system makes a rental unit uninhabitable during winter, forcing the tenant to vacate. The tenant may claim:

answers.text: adverse possession of the property due to the landlord's sustained neglect
full abatement of all rent owed from the date the tenancy began
constructive eviction, permitting termination of the lease and a claim for damages
a court-ordered specific performance requiring the landlord to repair immediately

explanations.a: Adverse possession requires open, hostile, continuous use over a statutory period; it is not a remedy for habitability failures.
explanations.b: Rent abatement may be a remedy, but typically only from the date the conditions became uninhabitable, not from the beginning of the tenancy.
explanations.c: Constructive eviction occurs when a landlord's acts or omissions so substantially impair the tenant's enjoyment that the tenant is forced to vacate; the tenant may then terminate the lease and seek damages.
explanations.d: Specific performance is rarely granted in landlord-tenant disputes for repairs; the practical remedy is constructive eviction or rent abatement.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A real estate investor who operates as a sole proprietor faces which of the following significant disadvantages?

answers.text: unlimited personal liability for all business debts and obligations
mandatory double taxation on profits distributed from the business
a requirement to register annually with the state corporation commission
a prohibition on entering into contracts with other businesses or individuals

explanations.a: A sole proprietor's personal assets are at risk because there is no legal separation between the owner and the business entity.
explanations.b: Double taxation is associated with C corporations; sole proprietors report business income on their personal tax returns without a second layer of taxation.
explanations.c: Sole proprietors face minimal registration requirements compared to corporations; formal annual registration is generally not required.
explanations.d: Sole proprietors may freely enter into contracts; there is no prohibition on contracting.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: In a limited partnership that holds real estate, the limited partners differ from the general partner in that limited partners:

answers.text: must personally manage all day-to-day operations of the partnership
are entitled to a greater share of profits as compensation for management duties
are personally liable for all debts and obligations of the partnership
risk losing only the amount of their capital contribution

explanations.a: The general partner manages the partnership; limited partners may not participate in management or they risk losing their limited liability protection.
explanations.b: Limited partners receive a share of profits based on their investment, not a management premium.
explanations.c: Unlimited personal liability applies to general partners, not limited partners.
explanations.d: A limited partner's liability is capped at the amount invested, which is the core advantage of limited partnership status.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: One primary advantage of holding investment real estate in a limited liability company (LLC) rather than as a sole proprietor is that:

answers.text: all losses from the property are permanently disregarded for federal income tax purposes
members are generally shielded from personal liability for the entity's debts and judgments
the LLC pays no federal income taxes on rental income under any circumstances
title transfers between LLC members are fully exempt from all state recording requirements

explanations.a: Losses are not permanently disregarded; they may pass through to members subject to tax rules on passive activity and basis limitations.
explanations.b: An LLC separates the members' personal assets from the entity's liabilities, protecting members from personal responsibility for business debts.
explanations.c: A single-member LLC is typically treated as a disregarded entity and pays no separate entity-level income tax, but rental income is still taxable at the member level.
explanations.d: Title transfers, even between members, may require recording and may trigger transfer taxes depending on state law.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A property owner who borrows money and pledges her property as collateral creates a lien BEST classified as:

answers.text: an involuntary lien arising by operation of law without the owner's consent
a general lien attaching to all of the owner's real and personal property
a voluntary lien created by the property owner's own deliberate act
a statutory lien imposed automatically by a government taxing authority

explanations.a: An involuntary lien arises without the owner's consent, such as a judgment lien or tax lien; a mortgage is consensual.
explanations.b: A mortgage is a specific lien on the particular pledged property, not a general lien on all assets.
explanations.c: A mortgage lien is voluntary because the owner willingly grants it as part of a loan agreement.
explanations.d: Statutory liens imposed by taxing authorities, such as real property tax liens, are involuntary and non-consensual.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A general contractor completes a kitchen renovation and is not paid by the property owner. To protect the right to be paid, the contractor may file a:

answers.text: mechanic's lien against the real property on which the work was performed
deed restriction against future improvements on the property
quiet title action to gain ownership of the property
writ of attachment seizing the owner's unrelated bank accounts

explanations.a: A mechanic's lien is an involuntary lien available to contractors, subcontractors, and materialmen who supply labor or materials to real property and are not paid.
explanations.b: A deed restriction is a private land use control created by agreement, not a collection remedy for unpaid debts.
explanations.c: Quiet title is an action to clear title disputes; it is not a remedy for an unpaid contractor.
explanations.d: A writ of attachment is a pre-judgment remedy that may be available, but a mechanic's lien is the specific remedy designed for unpaid construction work.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.keyword: first in time first in right
questions.text: A property has a first mortgage, a second mortgage, and a judgment lien, all properly recorded. The property is sold at a foreclosure sale with insufficient proceeds to satisfy all claims. In what order are the lienholders generally paid?

answers.text: the largest lien first, regardless of recording date
government liens first, then private liens in equal shares
all lienholders share the proceeds equally regardless of order
the lien recorded first in time is paid first, followed by later-recorded liens in sequence

explanations.a: Lien priority is determined by recording date, not amount; a small first mortgage takes priority over a larger second mortgage.
explanations.b: Government tax liens have a special priority status in some cases, but private lien priority generally follows recording order, not a government-first rule.
explanations.c: Pro-rata sharing regardless of priority would undermine the recording system that protects secured lenders.
explanations.d: The general rule of lien priority is 'first in time, first in right' — earlier-recorded liens are satisfied before later ones.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: An easement is BEST described as:

answers.text: a temporary lease of the right to enter another person's land for commercial purposes
an encroachment that must be resolved by a court order to remove
a non-possessory right to use another party's real property for a specific purpose
a government taking of private land requiring payment of just compensation

explanations.a: An easement is not a lease; it is a right of use without possession or a landlord-tenant relationship.
explanations.b: An encroachment is a physical intrusion on another's property and is a separate concept from an easement.
explanations.c: An easement grants a right to use another's land for a specific purpose — such as access or utilities — without possessing it.
explanations.d: Government takings occur through eminent domain; easements are private property interests, though government entities may also hold easements.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: An easement appurtenant differs from an easement in gross in that an easement appurtenant:

answers.text: benefits a specific named individual rather than a parcel of land
is attached to a dominant estate and automatically transfers when the benefited land is sold
expires automatically after a set number of years regardless of continued use
can be sold or transferred separately from any real property

explanations.a: An easement that benefits only a named individual is an easement in gross, not an easement appurtenant.
explanations.b: An easement appurtenant is attached to the dominant estate (the benefiting parcel) and runs with that land — it transfers automatically to new owners when the dominant estate is sold.
explanations.c: Easements do not automatically expire after a set number of years unless created with that specific limitation.
explanations.d: An easement in gross, not an appurtenant easement, is the type that may be transferred independently of land ownership.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A tenant who holds a valid lease on a rental property has the legal right to:

answers.text: remain in possession and enforce the lease against a new owner who purchases the property
purchase the property at current market value when it is listed for sale
receive a full refund of rent paid if the property is sold before the lease expires
negotiate entirely new lease terms directly with the new owner upon the sale

explanations.a: A valid lease is an encumbrance on title; a buyer who purchases subject to a lease takes the property with the tenant's right of possession intact through the lease term.
explanations.b: A lease does not create a right of first refusal or an option to purchase unless the lease specifically grants one.
explanations.c: A sale of the property does not entitle the tenant to a rent refund; the tenancy continues under the same terms.
explanations.d: A new owner is generally bound by the existing lease terms; renegotiation requires the consent of both parties.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A property survey reveals that a neighbor's storage shed extends three feet over the property line onto an adjacent owner's land. This intrusion is known as:

answers.text: an easement by prescription acquired through long-term use
an adverse possession claim that has already ripened into title
a deed condition that runs with the land indefinitely
an encroachment on the adjacent owner's property

explanations.a: A prescriptive easement requires open, hostile, continuous use for the statutory period; a survey discovery alone does not establish this.
explanations.b: Adverse possession is a claim requiring open, notorious, and continuous use; mere encroachment does not automatically transfer title.
explanations.c: A deed condition is a restriction written into a deed by a grantor, not a physical intrusion by a neighbor.
explanations.d: An encroachment is any structure, improvement, or object that illegally intrudes onto another's property beyond the boundary line.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A deed restriction on all lots in a subdivision prohibits commercial use. A homeowner begins operating a retail business from the property in violation of the restriction. Neighboring homeowners most appropriately may seek:

answers.text: damages from the county zoning board for approving the business license
adverse possession of the violating homeowner's property as a remedy
a court injunction to enforce the deed restriction and stop the commercial use
rescission of the original deed conveying the property to the violating owner

explanations.a: The zoning board does not enforce private deed restrictions; that is a matter for the courts.
explanations.b: Adverse possession is not a remedy for a deed restriction violation.
explanations.c: Private deed restrictions are enforced through equitable remedies in court, most commonly an injunction ordering the violating party to cease the prohibited use.
explanations.d: Rescission of a deed is not available as a remedy for a restriction violation; the court enforces the restriction rather than voiding the conveyance.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A homeowners association (HOA) may typically take all of the following enforcement actions EXCEPT:

answers.text: assessing fines and late fees for violations of the CC&Rs
imposing criminal penalties including incarceration for repeated violations
placing a lien against a member's property for unpaid assessments
filing a civil lawsuit to compel compliance with community rules

explanations.a: Assessing fines is a standard civil enforcement tool available to HOAs under their governing documents.
explanations.b: An HOA is a private civil entity with no authority to arrest or imprison members; criminal penalties are reserved for the state.
explanations.c: Most states allow HOAs to lien a member's property for delinquent dues and assessments.
explanations.d: Filing a civil lawsuit to seek injunctive relief or damages is a legitimate HOA enforcement tool.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires places of public accommodation and commercial facilities to:

answers.text: provide reasonable accommodations and remove architectural barriers to accessibility
guarantee employment to all qualified persons with disabilities on the premises
install elevators in every multi-story building regardless of cost or feasibility
allow any disabled tenant to permanently alter the rental unit at the tenant's expense

explanations.a: The ADA requires places of public accommodation to remove barriers and provide reasonable accommodations so that persons with disabilities have equal access to goods and services.
explanations.b: Employment discrimination is covered by a separate ADA title; the public accommodation provisions focus on access to facilities, not employment guarantees.
explanations.c: Elevators are required where readily achievable; the ADA does not mandate them in every multi-story building regardless of cost.
explanations.d: Reasonable modifications to units may be required under the Fair Housing Act for residential dwellings; the ADA covers public accommodations, not residential tenancies.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A property owner whose land is zoned for single-family residential use wishes to operate a small daycare center on the property. She should apply to the local zoning authority for:

answers.text: a deed restriction amendment approved by all neighboring owners
a special warranty deed that would expand the permitted uses
an eminent domain proceeding to reclassify the zone
a special-use permit or variance to allow a non-conforming use

explanations.a: Deed restriction amendments require consent of benefited parties, and would not change the zoning classification.
explanations.b: A special warranty deed is a form of deed that limits the grantor's title warranty; it does not affect land use regulations.
explanations.c: Eminent domain is a government power to take private property; a property owner cannot initiate an eminent domain proceeding to change zoning.
explanations.d: A variance or special-use permit allows the property owner to use the land in a manner not otherwise permitted by the base zoning, subject to the zoning authority's approval.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A city enacts an ordinance limiting building heights to protect scenic mountain views, which effectively reduces what an owner can build on her lot. The city is exercising which governmental power, and is compensation generally owed?

answers.text: eminent domain, which always requires just compensation to the affected owner
the taxing power, which requires compensation when it reduces property values
police power, which generally requires no compensation for reasonable regulatory restrictions
escheat, the power that reclaims abandoned or ownerless property for the state

explanations.a: Eminent domain involves a physical taking of title or possession; a height restriction is a regulatory limitation, not a taking requiring compensation.
explanations.b: Taxing power raises revenue; it does not apply to land use regulations.
explanations.c: Police power allows government to regulate land use for health, safety, and welfare without paying compensation, so long as the regulation is reasonable and does not constitute a regulatory taking.
explanations.d: Escheat applies to ownerless property reverting to the state; it has nothing to do with land use regulations.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: When the government exercises its power of eminent domain to take private property for a public use, the Fifth Amendment requires that the property owner receive:

answers.text: a replacement property of equal or greater market value
just compensation, typically measured by the property's fair market value
the highest comparable sales price recorded in the county within the past year
reimbursement for all relocation costs and lost business profits without limit

explanations.a: The government is not required to provide a replacement property; it must pay fair monetary compensation.
explanations.b: Just compensation is generally defined as the fair market value of the property taken — the price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller in an arm's-length transaction.
explanations.c: The highest recent comparable sale is not the constitutional standard; fair market value considers all relevant evidence, not the maximum.
explanations.d: Relocation assistance may be available under statute, but the constitutional requirement is simply just compensation — not unlimited reimbursement.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: A municipality levies a special assessment against all properties fronting a newly constructed sidewalk. A special assessment differs from a general ad valorem property tax in that a special assessment:

answers.text: is levied only against properties that receive a specific, direct benefit from the public improvement
is based solely on the income-producing potential of each affected property
is payable to the state government rather than to the local municipality
is always deductible from federal income taxes as an ordinary business expense

explanations.a: A special assessment is a charge imposed on properties that receive a particular, direct benefit from a specific public improvement — such as a street, sidewalk, or sewer — distinguishing it from a general property tax.
explanations.b: Special assessments are based on the benefit conferred, not on income potential; that distinction is relevant to income-based taxes.
explanations.c: Special assessments are typically levied and collected by local governments, not the state.
explanations.d: The deductibility of special assessments depends on whether they are allocable to a capital improvement or a current-period benefit; a blanket deduction rule does not apply.

questions.name: Real Property Ownership and Interest
questions.text: When a developer proposes to divide a large tract of land into residential lots for sale, local governments typically require the developer to:

answers.text: guarantee the resale value of all homes constructed in the subdivision for a minimum of five years
permanently restrict all lots to single-family residential use by state statute
obtain approval from the state real estate commission before recording any deeds
submit a subdivision plat for government review and obtain approval before selling any individual lots

explanations.a: No law requires developers to guarantee resale values; that is a market and contract matter.
explanations.b: Land use restrictions may be applied through zoning or CC&Rs, but there is no blanket state statute permanently restricting all subdivisions.
explanations.c: Real estate commissions license brokers and salespersons; they do not approve subdivision plats.
explanations.d: Subdivision regulations require developers to have a plat reviewed and approved by the local planning or zoning authority before lots can be sold, ensuring compliance with infrastructure and land use standards.
